worst_places.problem: css-html-quiz-11, selector `.container > div.active:hover`. There is one pseudo-class, not two, and the `div` type selector is never counted. The correct value is 0-3-1 — which is option 1, sitting right there unused, while `correctIndex: 0` marks the wrong 0-2-2. The invented second pseudo-class exists only to make the wrong total add up, so a reader who follows the reasoning learns a broken counting rule. css-html-quiz-26 is the same failure with no escape hatch: its explanation correctly counts '3 class/attribute selectors' plus an uncounted `div`, giving 0-3-1, but 0-3-1 is not among the four options at all.
worst_places.before: The specificity is calculated as (IDs, classes, pseudo-classes/elements). This selector has 2 classes (.container, .active), 2 pseudo-classes (:hover is a pseudo-class, not pseudo-element), and 0 IDs, giving 0-2-2. The child combinator (>) does not affect specificity.
worst_places.after: Specificity is counted in three columns: (IDs, classes+attributes+pseudo-classes, elements+pseudo-elements). This selector has 0 IDs; `.container`, `.active` and `:hover` fill the middle column, giving 3; and `div` is one element, giving 1. So the value is 0-3-1. The child combinator (`>`) adds nothing. (Fix `correctIndex` to 1.)

worst_places.after: Which property creates a new stacking context with no other visual side effect? … `isolation: isolate`. All three options create a stacking context, but the other two pay for it: `opacity: 0.99` makes the element very slightly transparent, and `will-change: transform` keeps a compositor layer alive in GPU memory. `isolation: isolate` does nothing except create the context. Note that creating a context always confines descendant z-index values to it — that is the point of using it. (Fix `correctIndex` to 0.)

worst_places.quote: `position: relative` (along with many other properties like `opacity < 1`, `transform`, or `display: flex`) creates a new stacking context.
worst_places.problem: css-html-quiz-15. `display: flex` does not create a stacking context (a flex *item* with a z-index does; the container does not), and `position: relative` alone does not either — which css-html-quiz-5 in the same file correctly states. Article 05 gives the authoritative list and `display: flex` is absent from it. The item is confused a second way: the question asks why `.dropdown` sits behind `.modal` 'despite having a lower z-index' (999 vs 1000 — that is simply the expected outcome, not a puzzle), while the explanation ends 'even with a higher z-index number'. Question and explanation describe opposite scenarios.
worst_places.before: A stacking context is an isolated rendering layer where z-index values are compared locally, not globally. `position: relative` (along with many other properties like `opacity < 1`, `transform`, or `display: flex`) creates a new stacking context.
worst_places.after: A stacking context is an isolated rendering layer: z-index values inside it are compared only with each other, never with elements outside it. `position: relative` creates one only when `z-index` is not `auto` — here `z-index: 1000` does it. Some properties create one on their own, with no `position` at all: `opacity` below 1, `transform`, `filter`, `will-change`, `isolation: isolate`.

worst_places.before: **Common pitfall:** forgetting that `container-type: size` or `inline-size` also forces the container's own size containment (it can no longer size itself based on its children along that axis) — so you usually need to give the container an explicit width/height or a layout context (grid track, flex basis) that determines its size independently, otherwise you get a circular sizing problem where the container and its content are each waiting on the other.
worst_places.after: **Common pitfall:** forgetting that `container-type: size` and `inline-size` also switch on size containment for the container itself. Along that axis the container can no longer measure its own children to decide its size. If nothing else sets that size, the container waits for its content and the content waits for the container — a circular sizing problem, and the query never fires. So give the container an explicit `width`/`height`, or put it somewhere that sizes it from outside: a grid track, or a flex item with a `flex-basis`.

patterns: The quiz answer key is broken at scale, and the explanations are where it shows. 13 of 30 items have an `explanation` that contradicts its own `correctIndex`, miscounts, or answers a different question than the one asked: quiz-2, 5, 8, 11, 12, 15, 17, 21, 22, 26, 27, 29 plus quiz-1's mis-stated (1,3,1). Two of them (quiz-2, quiz-8) contain unedited model self-talk — 'Wait, let me recalculate', 'I apologize—let me verify' — and quiz-26 has no correct option among its four. Because rubric C is scored on the explanation, this alone puts the quiz at C=1: a reader who trusts the explanation is actively taught the wrong answer. Layered on top, the key is guessable without reading: `correctIndex` is 0 in 21 of 30 items (70%; 3 each for 1, 2 and 3), and in 14 of those the index-0 option is also the longest — 'pick the first, longest option' scores about 70%.

The bank is strong on C and weak on E in the same specific way: it always tells you the rule and rarely shows you the result. Only 13 of 48 answers put a rendered outcome inside a code comment (`/* rendered width: 200 + 20*2 + 2*2 = 244px */` in q-1, `auto-fill -> 3 items stay 200px wide` in q-21, `/* desugars to: .card:hover */` in q-38); the other 35 use comments that label *intent* ('horizontal centering', 'creates a positioning context') and leave the visual outcome to be imagined. The habit thins out as difficulty rises — 6/20 junior answers state an outcome, 1/8 advanced ones — so the questions that most need a picture (q-31 stacking order, q-39 subgrid footer alignment, q-35 container queries, q-40 the transition pseudo-element tree) have none. There is not a single box-drawing diagram in all 48 answers, even though articles 02, 03 and 04 use them for the very same box model, flexbox and auto-fit topics.

One contiguous block of the bank was authored from a mislabelled template: every code fence in css-html-q-21 through q-30 is tagged ```typescript, in both locales. 18 of those 19 blocks contain plain CSS or HTML, so the reader gets CSS coloured as TypeScript on a phone. It is a mechanical, zero-risk fix confined to ten entries, and the correct labels (```css, ```html, ```javascript) are already used correctly everywhere else in the file.
notes: RU/EN asymmetry runs opposite to the articles. In the question bank RU is complete (0.92 of EN word count, nothing dropped) and is the *easier* locale: 31.9% long sentences vs 44.4% EN, no 70-word sentences, and almost no calques. EN is harder — idioms a B1-B2 reader will stall on ('belt-and-suspenders', 'trips people up', 'eat into', 'warm up a connection'), plus four EN-only unexpanded acronyms (CJK, FLIP, VRAM, CPU). The bank RU's own weakness is untranslated English nouns inflected into Russian: «скроллящемуся предку», «неслоёные/слоёные стили», «стилшитах», «тем-зависимых», «лейаута», and «вьюпорт» vs «viewport» used inconsistently across entries. The quiz reverses this: RU is the weaker locale there (G=2) — it drops clarifying words (quiz-19 'screen reader context' -> «контекста экрана», quiz-27 loses the entire flex derivation), and translates one CSS box four different ways. Its one advantage is accidental: the self-talk in quiz-2 and quiz-8 was cleaned out of RU while the wrong `correctIndex` was left in both. Verdict is systemic-refactor because of the quiz alone; the 48-question bank on its own would be targeted-fixes (C=5, answer-first throughout, same strength the articles showed).
